span.label: The human fMRI evidence reviewed rests on a signal whose neural basis is not understood.
span.note: what this limits: the human fMRI evidence reviewed: THE NEURAL UNDERPINNINGS OF THE MEASURED BLOOD OXYGEN LEVEL DEPENDENT (BOLD) SIGNAL ARE UNCLEAR

span.label: The paper names the inference its measurements do not license, not merely the uncertainty.
span.note: what this limits: any reading of a BOLD prediction-error signal as dopamine: the authors state that one cannot interpret BOLD measurements as reflecting dopaminergic activity per se, despite dopamine's possible direct effect on the signal

span.note: the first is the NORMATIVE FRAMEWORK WITHIN WHICH the second is analysed and interpreted - a lens applied to a phenomenon. It is not `operationalised-as` (the phenomenon is not measured as the framework), not `causes`, not `is-a`, and not `part-of`; the relation is 'X is the standard by which Y is read'

span.label: the BOLD signal, here - NOT A DOPAMINE MEASUREMENT: dopamine may affect BOLD directly, and the authors state one still cannot interpret BOLD as reflecting dopaminergic activity per se, so the prediction-error signal seen in human imaging and the dopaminergic signal recorded in animals are two different measurements that the review keeps apart
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: the caveat's symmetry - STATED IN BOTH DIRECTIONS: the same coupling that makes BOLD hard to interpret makes dopamine worth measuring directly, and the paper says so rather than reporting only the half that limits it

span.label: the RL framework - NORMATIVE, AND USED INTERPRETIVELY: it provides a framework for what an optimal agent should do, and is applied to analyse and interpret what animals actually did; the same structure kahneman-tversky1979 names for expected utility theory, which is accepted as a normative model and applied as a descriptive one
